Add an Instance Editable variable named BossDiedReference with the type BP_BossDied Object Reference. On BeginPlay, use Assign OnBossDied on that reference, and make the new event call Toggle Visibility on the Point Light. Epic's guide uses an explosion Blueprint from the Starter Content here, which current engine versions no longer include.
Place the door and 3 alarm lights in the level. On each one, set BossDiedReference to the BP_BossDied you placed. Press Play and walk into the box.
Extra: on one alarm light, add an Unbind All Events node after it reacts. Walk into the box a second time. The other lights switch off again, and this one stays on because it no longer listens.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Make an Actor Blueprint named BP_Showcase with a Static Mesh Component, and set Auto Receive Input to Player 0 in its Class Defaults so that it receives key presses. Add a variable named HeavyMesh with the type Static Mesh, choose Soft Object Reference, and make it Instance Editable. Place a copy in the level and assign a mesh to HeavyMesh on that copy. In a real game this would be a large mesh. For the test any mesh works, for example SM_Ramp from the folder LevelPrototyping/Meshes of the template.

Right-click BP_Showcase in the Content Browser and open the Reference Viewer, which shows the assets it depends on. Take a screenshot. Then change HeavyMesh to a hard Object Reference, assign the mesh again, and take a second screenshot of the Reference Viewer. Compare the two.

Set the variable back to Soft Object Reference. Add an event for the L key: first check Is Valid Soft Object Reference, then call Async Load Asset. On its Completed pin, call Set Static Mesh with the loaded object and print Loaded.

Add a variable named SpawnClass with the type Actor and choose Soft Class Reference. Add an event for the K key that calls Async Load Class Asset and then uses Spawn Actor from Class with the result at the location of the actor.

Add an event for the B key that uses Load Asset Blocking instead. Open stat unit, and press B right after you start a fresh Play In Editor session. Then start again and press L. Write one line that says which one made the game hitch.

Add a second soft mesh variable and load both meshes one after the other. Write two lines: why the loaded mesh stays in memory after Set Static Mesh, and what would happen to a loaded object that nothing holds a hard reference to.
Create a new project named UC_Sandbox from the Third Person template. Choose Blueprint as the project type and leave the other settings as they are.
Press Play and run around the level once.
Create and open a second project from the Blank template and compare the two. Notice that Blank has no pawn (no character to control) and no level art.
Close the Blank project. You can keep UC_Sandbox as a place to practice, but you do not have to: every quest tells you which template to start from.

quiz.q: When you create a new project you pick a template. What does the Third Person template give you that the Blank template does not?
choices: A character you can play, a camera, input controls and a sample level
A project that only uses C++
quiz.explain: Third Person comes with a ready-made character and a small level, so you can press Play and walk around straight away.

quiz.q: When is the Blank template the right one to pick?
choices: When you want to build every system yourself, with nothing made for you
Only when you make a mobile game
quiz.explain: Blank is empty on purpose. It is the right start when you do not want any ready-made character, camera or level in your way.

quiz.q: The new-project window asks you to choose between Blueprint and C++. What does this choice decide?
choices: Whether the project starts with C++ source files
Which platform it is built for
quiz.explain: It only decides what the project starts with. A Blueprint project can still have C++ added to it later.

quiz.q: Old tutorials tell you to tick a Starter Content checkbox in the new-project window. You cannot find it in a current Unreal Engine version. Why?
choices: Current versions no longer include the Starter Content pack
It only appears for C++ projects
It only appears in the Blank template
quiz.explain: Starter Content was a pack of sample meshes, materials and sounds. Current engine versions no longer include it, so the quests here use the assets of the templates and of the engine.

quiz.q: You want a game where the camera looks down on the character from above. Which template gives you that as a starting point?
quiz.explain: The Top Down template starts with a character that is seen from above. First Person shows the world through the eyes of the character, and Third Person puts the camera behind the character.

checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open the Content Drawer with Ctrl+Space. This is the panel that shows all the files of your project.
Create a folder at /Content/UC/ and add these subfolders inside it: Maps, Meshes, Materials, Textures, and Blueprints.

Rename or duplicate one asset of each kind so that it has the correct prefix: SM_ for a Static Mesh, M_ for a material, MI_ for a Material Instance, T_ for a texture, BP_ for a Blueprint, and L_ for a level. You can copy assets from the template folders, such as LevelPrototyping and Characters, into your folders for this.
Save a level with the name L_Sandbox in the folder UC/Maps.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Find a material that has parameters. The template has one: M_PrototypeGrid in the folder LevelPrototyping/Materials.
Right-click the material, choose Create Material Instance, and name the new asset MI_Wall_Accent.
Open the instance and change one parameter in it, such as a color or the roughness.
Apply the instance to one wall in your level, for example by dragging it onto the wall. If your level has no wall, place a cube from the Place Actors panel, scale it into a wall, and use that.

quiz.q: Your system came from the Simple Sprite Burst template. What must change so it draws a ribbon?
choices: Delete the Sprite Renderer and add a Ribbon Renderer
quiz.explain: The template uses a Sprite Renderer. The tutorial deletes it and adds a Ribbon Renderer.

quiz.q: DefaultRibbonMaterial does not show in the Material dropdown. What do you do?
choices: In View Options, turn on Show Engine Content and Show Plugin Content
quiz.explain: The material is plugin content. Show Engine Content and Show Plugin Content make it visible.

quiz.q: Why set Emitter State Life Cycle Mode to System here?
choices: The system then calculates life cycle settings, which usually optimizes performance
It is required for any ribbon
quiz.explain: Self mode is for full custom life cycle logic. System mode lets the system handle it, which usually optimizes performance.

quiz.q: The ribbon should be one continuous stream, not a single burst. Which module gives that?
quiz.explain: Spawn Rate creates a continuous stream of particles while the emitter is active.

quiz.q: Acceleration Force Z is set to -200. What happens if you make it +200?
choices: The ribbon spirals upward instead of falling
quiz.explain: A negative Z makes the ribbon drop. A positive Z makes it spiral upward.

quiz.q: What does UV0 Tiling Distance do on a Ribbon Renderer?
choices: Tiles UV channel 0 by the distance the ribbon travels, and turns off UV offset by age
Changes the draw order of emitters
quiz.explain: It tiles UV0 based on distance traveled. This disables offsetting the UVs by age.

quiz.q: When does Draw Direction usually make a visible difference?
choices: When the material is translucent and the ribbon folds on itself
quiz.explain: The reference says Draw Direction usually matters only for translucent materials where the ribbon folds on itself.

quiz.q: With Tessellation Mode set to Custom, what does a smaller Tessellation Angle do?
quiz.explain: Smaller Tessellation Angle values increase the amount of tessellation.
